To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the activity of the enzyme deoxycytidylate kinase is regulated by protein phosphorylation in leukemic cells, and that this regulation can be exploited to enhance nucleoside analogs that are used in cancer chemotherapy.

the activation of deoxycyctidine kinase (dck) by 2-chlorodeoxyadenosine in leukemic cells can be increased in the presence of okadaic acid, a protein phosphatase 2A (pp2a) inhibitor, or of protein kinase inhibitors, such as genistein, PD-98056 and U-0124, which inhibit tyrosine kinases and mitogen activated protein kinases (mapk).
dCK activity in leukemic cells is regulated through reversible phosphorylations, and that the MAPK/Erk pathway and protein phosphatase 2A are involved in this process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of dCTP synthesis and the role that dCTP plays in the regulation of DNA synthesis and repair.
the activation of the enzyme deoxycytidylate kinase in leukemic cells and how it is regulated by protein kinases.
the activation of dC kinase by protein kinase and protein phosphatase inhibitors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dCK is regulated by protein phosphorylation and dephosphorylation in a complex and not fully understood mechanism.
the activity of the deoxycytosine kinase is regulated by a complex mechanism involving protein kinases, protein phosphatases, and other regulatory factors, which are still not well characterized.

the activation of the MAP kinase pathway by CdA in EHEB cells is associated with an increased activity of dCK and this activation of the MAPK pathway is not dependent upon the activation of JAK2 or JAK3.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
protein tyrosine kinases, the JAK/MARK pathway and PP2A might be involved in the activation of dCk in leukemic cells.
dCK activity can be regulated through reversible protein phosphorylation and that this mechanism is involved in the activation of dck by CdA and other protein kinase inhibitors.
dCK activity can be regulated by protein phosphorylation and dephosphorylation, which may be a mechanism of regulation of this enzyme in normal and leukemic cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

dCK activity can be enhanced by inhibition of protein phosphatases and activation of specific kinases, which may lead to a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation and activity of dCK.
